descripcion_es: Generic reference, institutions (school, hospital, prison), abstract nouns and geographical names.
resumen: English leaves out the article when it talks in general with plurals or uncountable nouns (Life is short), unlike Spanish. The appears when something is specific or identifiable, and some institutions change their meaning with or without the article.

explicacion.texto: Generalisation: plural or uncountable noun without an article. Dogs are loyal. Unemployment is rising. Money doesn't bring happiness. In Spanish we would say “los perros”, “el paro”, “el dinero”.
If the noun is made specific (with of, a relative clause or the context), it takes the: The unemployment of the 1930s was devastating. The money I lent you.

filas: He's in hospital. (admitted as a patient)
I visited him at the hospital. (I went to the building)
She goes to school. (she is a pupil)
Her mother went to the school to see the teacher.
He was sent to prison. (as a prisoner)
The journalists went to the prison.
We go to church on Sundays. (to attend Mass)
The church in our village is Romanesque.
go to bed / go to work / be at university
the bed is broken / the university campus

items: The + singular countable noun for a class or species, especially in formal style: The tiger is endangered. The computer changed our lives.
The + adjective for groups of people: the rich, the elderly, the unemployed (plural verb).
Musical instruments with the: play the guitar. Sports without an article: play tennis.
Meals, days and seasons in general without an article: have lunch, on Monday, in winter.

Geographical names: no article with countries, cities, lakes and single mountains (France, Lake Como, Everest); the with rivers, seas, mountain ranges, archipelagos and countries with plural names or with republic/kingdom (the Thames, the Alps, the Canaries, the USA, the UK).

ejemplos.traduccion: La naturaleza es la mejor maestra.

ejemplos.frase: The history of this town goes back to Roman times.
ejemplos.traduccion: La historia de este pueblo se remonta a la época romana.

ejemplos.frase: My grandfather has been in hospital since Tuesday.
ejemplos.traduccion: Mi abuelo está ingresado desde el martes.

ejemplos.frase: The elderly are especially vulnerable to heatwaves.
ejemplos.traduccion: Las personas mayores son especialmente vulnerables a las olas de calor.

ejemplos.frase: The bicycle is still the most efficient means of transport.
ejemplos.traduccion: La bicicleta sigue siendo el medio de transporte más eficiente.

ejemplos.frase: We sailed down the Danube and then crossed the Black Sea.
ejemplos.traduccion: Bajamos el Danubio en barco y luego cruzamos el mar Negro.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: The life is full of surprises.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Abstract nouns in a general sense take no article.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: The women earn less than the men in many countries.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Women earn less than men in many countries.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Generalisation with a plural: no article.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: My brother is in the prison.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: If you are talking about the function (being in prison as a prisoner), no article.

ejercicios.frase: ___ is the main concern of most households.
ejercicios.explicacion: The generalisation rule in the sheet applies: plural or uncountable noun without an article when speaking in general. The clue is that “inflation” refers to the phenomenon in general, without anything making it specific (there is no “of…” or relative clause after it). So “Inflation is the main concern”, without an article, although Spanish says “la inflación”. Compare with the next exercise, where it is made specific.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Abstract noun in a general sense: no article.
ejercicios.traduccion: La inflación es la principal preocupación de la mayoría de los hogares.

por_opcion.Inflation: Correct: abstract noun in a general sense, no article.
por_opcion.The inflation: Incorrect: it is a literal translation of Spanish “la inflación”; it would only be correct if it were made specific (“the inflation of the 1970s”).
por_opcion.An inflation: Incorrect: “inflation” is uncountable in this use and does not take “an”.

ejercicios.frase: ___ inflation of the 1970s was caused partly by oil prices.
ejercicios.explicacion: The second rule in the sheet applies: if the noun is made specific with of, a relative clause or the context, it takes the. The clue is “of the 1970s”, which defines which inflation we are talking about: that of a specific period. So “The inflation of the 1970s”, with a capital letter at the start of the sentence (lower case is also accepted). It is the exact contrast with the previous exercise.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Specific inflation (that of the seventies): the.
ejercicios.traduccion: La inflación de los años setenta se debió en parte a los precios del petróleo.

errores_previstos.respuesta: An
errores_previstos.explicacion: “Inflation” is uncountable and here it is made specific: it takes “the”, not “an”.

errores_previstos.respuesta: A
errores_previstos.explicacion: Neither “a” nor “an” fits an uncountable noun that has been made specific; you need “the”.

ejercicios.frase: The government should do more to help ___ homeless.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule in the sheet of the + adjective to refer to a group of people applies: the rich, the elderly, the unemployed. The clue is “homeless”, an adjective (without a home) that works here as a collective noun. To do that it needs “the”, and the group is treated as plural. No -s is added to the adjective: “the homeless”, not “the homelesses”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The + adjective for a group of people.
ejercicios.traduccion: El Gobierno debería hacer más para ayudar a las personas sin hogar.

errores_previstos.respuesta: a
errores_previstos.explicacion: “The homeless” refers to the group; “a” would require a countable noun (“a homeless person”).

errores_previstos.respuesta: those
errores_previstos.explicacion: “Those homeless” would be understood, but the exercise asks for the article and the fixed structure is “the homeless”.

ejercicios.frase: My daughter started ___ last September; she's studying law.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table of institutions in the sheet applies: no article when talking about their function (studying, being a patient, serving a sentence) and the when talking about the building. The clue is “she's studying law”: the daughter is starting her studies, not visiting a building. So “started university”, just like “be at university”. With “the university” you would be talking about a specific university as a place.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Start university = begin your degree: function, no article.
ejercicios.traduccion: Mi hija empezó la universidad el pasado septiembre; está estudiando Derecho.

por_opcion.university: Correct: function (starting university studies), no article.
por_opcion.the university: Incorrect here: it would refer to the building or to a specific university already known, not to the fact of starting a degree.
por_opcion.an university: Incorrect on two counts: no article is needed, and “university” begins with the sound /juː/, so it would be “a”, never “an”.

ejercicios.frase: ___ are more expensive than they were ten years ago.
ejercicios.explicacion: The generalisation rule applies: plural without an article when speaking in general. The clue is that the sentence compares house prices in general, not specific houses. So “Houses are more expensive”. Spanish says “las casas”, but in English “the houses” would point to particular houses (for example, the ones in this street).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: General statement with a plural: no article.
ejercicios.traduccion: Las casas son más caras que hace diez años.

por_opcion.Houses: Correct: plural in a general sense, no article.
por_opcion.The houses: Incorrect here: it would refer to specific houses already identified.
por_opcion.A houses: Incorrect: “a” never goes with a plural.

ejercicios.explicacion: The geographical rule in the sheet applies: countries take no article, except those with plural names or with republic or kingdom (the USA, the UK). The clue is the final -s of “Netherlands”, which shows it is a plural name. So “the Netherlands”, just like “the Philippines”. Spanish also says “los Países Bajos”, so here the two languages coincide.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Countries with plural names take the.
ejercicios.traduccion: ¿Has estado alguna vez en los Países Bajos?

por_opcion.the Netherlands: Correct: a country with a plural name, with “the”.
por_opcion.Netherlands: Incorrect: countries with plural names take “the”.
por_opcion.a Netherlands: Incorrect: “a” never goes with proper names of countries or with plurals.

ejercicios.frase: She plays ___ violin in an orchestra.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule in the sheet applies: musical instruments take the after “play” (play the guitar), unlike sports (play tennis). The clue is “violin”, an instrument. So “She plays the violin”. With “a violin” you would be talking about a particular violin as an object, not about the activity of playing that instrument.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Playing an instrument: play the + instrument.
ejercicios.traduccion: Toca el violín en una orquesta.

por_opcion.a: Incorrect: “play a violin” sounds like playing any violin as an object; for the activity you say “play the violin”.
por_opcion.sin artículo: Incorrect in standard British English. In informal American English you sometimes hear “play violin”, especially in professional contexts, but the rule in the sheet is “play the”.

ejercicios.explicacion: The geographical rule applies: single mountains take no article (Everest, Mont Blanc), mountain ranges take the (the Alps). The clue is that “Mont Blanc” is a specific mountain, not a range. So “We climbed Mont Blanc”. Spanish says “el Mont Blanc”, and that article is exactly the one you have to drop in English.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Single mountains take no article (mountain ranges do).
ejercicios.traduccion: El verano pasado subimos al Mont Blanc.

por_opcion.the Mont Blanc: Incorrect: it is a literal translation of Spanish “el Mont Blanc”; single mountains take no article.
por_opcion.a Mont Blanc: Incorrect: “a” does not go with proper names of unique places.

ejercicios.frase: The happiness is more important than money.
respuestas: Happiness is more important than money.
ejercicios.explicacion: The generalisation rule with abstract and uncountable nouns applies. The clue is that both “happiness” and “money” are used in a general sense, without being made specific. So “Happiness is more important than money”, with no article on either. Spanish says “la felicidad” and “el dinero”, which leads to the mistake of adding “the”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Abstract noun in general: no the.
ejercicios.traduccion: La felicidad es más importante que el dinero.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The happiness is more important than money.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: abstract nouns in a general sense take no article.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The happiness is more important than the money.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It adds another wrong “the”: neither “happiness” nor “money” is made specific, so neither takes an article.

ejercicios.frase: The cats are more independent than the dogs.
respuestas: Cats are more independent than dogs.
ejercicios.explicacion: The generalisation rule with plurals applies. The clue is that the sentence compares two species in general: it is not about particular cats or dogs. So you have to remove the article from both nouns: “Cats are more independent than dogs”. Correcting only one leaves the sentence half done.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Generalisation with plurals: no article on either of them.
ejercicios.traduccion: Los gatos son más independientes que los perros.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The cats are more independent than the dogs.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: in a generalisation neither of the two plurals takes an article.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Cats are more independent than the dogs.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Only one of the two articles has been removed; “the dogs” is still a mistake.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The cats are more independent than dogs.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Only the second one has been corrected; “the cats” is also unnecessary.

ejercicios.frase: The thief was sent to the prison for three years.
respuestas: The thief was sent to prison for three years.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table of institutions applies: no article when talking about the function (being a prisoner), the when talking about the building. The clue is “was sent to … for three years”: the thief is sent to serve a sentence, which is the function of a prison. So “sent to prison”. “Sent to the prison” would suggest someone sent to the building for another reason, for example a journalist.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: With prison in its function (serving a sentence), no article is used.
ejercicios.traduccion: Condenaron al ladrón a tres años de cárcel.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The thief was sent to the prison for three years.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: for serving a sentence you say “to prison”, without an article.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The thief was sent to a prison for three years.
errores_previstos.explicacion: “A prison” focuses on any building; the expression for the sentence is “sent to prison”.

ejercicios.frase: We spent a week sailing around Canary Islands.
respuestas: We spent a week sailing around the Canary Islands.
ejercicios.explicacion: The geographical rule applies: rivers, seas, mountain ranges and archipelagos take the. The clue is “Canary Islands”, an archipelago with a plural name. So “around the Canary Islands”, just like “the Balearic Islands” or simply “the Canaries”. What takes no article is each single island: “Tenerife”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Pasamos una semana navegando por las islas Canarias.

errores_previstos.respuesta: We spent a week sailing around Canary Islands.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: archipelagos take “the”.

errores_previstos.respuesta: We spent a week sailing around the Canary Island.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The archipelago is plural, “Islands”; you also need to keep it for “the” to make sense.

ejercicios.enunciado: Rewrite the sentence in a general sense with a plural without an article.
ejercicios.frase: The smartphone has changed the way we communicate.
respuestas: Smartphones have changed the way we communicate.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule in the sheet linking two ways of talking about a class applies: the + singular countable noun (more formal, “The smartphone has changed…”) is equivalent to a plural without an article (“Smartphones have changed…”). The clue is that the sentence talks about the smartphone as an invention, not about a particular phone. When you change to the plural you have to remove “the”, add the -s and change the verb to “have”. “The way we communicate” keeps its article because it is made specific by the relative clause.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The + singular (species) is equivalent to a plural without an article; the verb becomes plural.
ejercicios.traduccion: Los teléfonos inteligentes han cambiado nuestra forma de comunicarnos.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The smartphones have changed the way we communicate.
errores_previstos.explicacion: In a general sense the plural takes no article; “the smartphones” would refer to particular phones.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Smartphones has changed the way we communicate.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The subject is now plural, so the auxiliary must be “have”, not “has”.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Smartphones have changed way we communicate.
errores_previstos.explicacion: “The way we communicate” does take the article: it is made specific by the clause that follows.

ejercicios.explicacion: The rule of the + adjective to refer to groups of people applies: the rich, the poor, the elderly. The clue is “poor”, an adjective that works as a collective noun and needs “the” in front. The order is subject “we” + modal “should” + verb “help” + “the poor”. The question “should we help the poor” is also accepted.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The + adjective refers to the group of people.

errores_previstos.respuesta: we should help poor the
errores_previstos.explicacion: The article goes before the adjective: “the poor”.

errores_previstos.respuesta: we help should the poor
errores_previstos.explicacion: The modal “should” goes before the main verb “help”.

ejercicios.explicacion: The table of institutions and places applies: go to bed (function, going to sleep) versus the bed (the piece of furniture). The clue is that there is no article among the words given, and none is needed: “go to bed” is a fixed expression. The order is subject “I” + “go to bed” + the adverb “early” at the end.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Go to bed without an article (function, not the piece of furniture).

errores_previstos.respuesta: I go early to bed
errores_previstos.explicacion: “Early” goes at the end, after the expression “go to bed”, which is not split.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Early I go to bed
errores_previstos.explicacion: It is a forced order; the natural thing is to leave “early” at the end of the sentence.

descripcion_larga_es: Advanced uses of articles: generalising without an article (Inflation is rising), making specific with the (the inflation of the 1970s), institutions with and without an article (in hospital versus at the hospital), the + adjective (the poor) and geographical names. It is one of the most persistent sources of error for Spanish speakers, because Spanish uses an article exactly where English does not want one.

contexto.que_es: These are the rules that go beyond basic a/an/the: when an abstract noun or a plural takes no article because you are speaking in general, when it takes the because it is made specific, how the meaning of school, hospital or prison changes with or without the article, the use of the + adjective for groups of people and the article with geographical names.
contexto.por_que_importa: These mistakes survive up to the highest levels and an examiner spots them straight away (“the life is…”, “the unemployment is rising”). Some change the meaning: “He's in prison” means he is a prisoner; “He's at the prison” means he has gone to the building. In formal writing and on economic topics (inflation, unemployment, growth) they come up in almost every sentence.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: Every time you generalise (statements about society, the economy, nature), or talk about institutions (school, university, hospital, prison, church), social groups (the rich, the unemployed) or geographical places. The signal to drop the article is the general sense; the signal to use it is something that makes the noun specific: of, a relative clause or the context. Spanish speakers, guided by “la inflación” or “los perros”, add the automatically.
